title: Rethinking KV Cache Eviction for Agentic LLM Serving
abstract: Key-value (KV) caches impose substantial memory pressure on large language model serving systems, requiring cache eviction when capacity is insufficient. Existing mechanisms typically evict KV from the ends of cached sequences to preserve prefix sharing across requests. However, agent workloads repeatedly reuse long histories across successive turns. Recomputing the KV cache for tokens near the end of a sequence is substantially more expensive than for earlier tokens because their attention computation involves longer histories. To address this problem, we propose preserving shared prefixes and evicting the KV cache from the beginning of the remaining history while retaining the cached suffix. We build Penelope around this strategy by co-designing the eviction policy, KV recomputation, and unified GPU-CPU cache management. Returning requests reuse the KV cache retained in GPU or CPU memory and recompute only missing segments while preserving reuse of the cached suffix. We implement Penelope in SGLang and evaluate it on three Qwen3 model sizes using real agent traces. Compared with SGLang, Penelope reduces mean time to first token by up to 60% and job completion time by up to 37% with a GPU-only cache, and by up to 76% and 60% with a two-tier GPU-CPU cache.

title: Understanding GPU Megakernels: Why Residency Can Mislead
abstract: Megakernels let one persistent GPU program prepare dependent operators early and execute ready tasks together. We study the benefits and costs of these capabilities by reconstructing two LLM megakernels, ThunderKittens (TK) and VDCores, as separate kernels on H100 using their original operator code. Our results show that CTA residency can misrepresent opportunities for useful overlap in both directions. By overlapping startup and operand loading with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), the reconstructions reduce decode-step latency by 5.7% in TK and achieve comparable performance in VDCores when both executions enforce the required memory ordering. Under whole-operator dependencies, TK's persistent execution still gains more from prefetch, but runtime and completion-signal ordering costs outweigh this advantage. Both startup overlap and prefetch depend on resource availability. Persistent CTAs can reuse storage before retiring, whereas separate successors must acquire their full CTA footprints before initializing or loading operands. This admission constraint in both reconstructions motivates finer resource sharing across kernels. Beyond early preparation, joint execution requires ready work and spare capacity in the bottleneck resource. Reserving SMs for communication can add GEMM waves that erase overlap gains, while filling idle SMs offers little benefit once memory bandwidth is saturated. These findings clarify benefits and costs of megakernels and motivate GPU support for earlier resource reuse across kernels.

title: Weights That Stay: On-Chip Megakernels for Serial Heads in Speculative Decoding
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Parallel speculative drafters use a lightweight serial head to recover token dependencies within a block generated in parallel. Each head step updates only a small state, yet projects that state through the same vocabulary-sized matrix. Step-wise execution repeatedly transfers this large, immutable projection, making the head a meaningful source of latency despite its low arithmetic cost. We present Weights That Stay, an execution design that keeps projection shards on chip for the entire serial draft walk. A persistent megakernel couples weight residency with GPU-side token selection and state advancement, reusing resident weights while exchanging only compact state between steps. The design supports full or partial residency and accommodates both Markov and recurrent heads on H100 and B200. Integrated into SGLang, Weights That Stay improves throughput for Markov drafting on Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B, with gains of up to 12.3%. At the head level, the DSpark walk is up to 11.6$\times$ faster than the fastest measured SGLang reference path. These results show that aligning weight residency with the full draft walk translates cross-step reuse into end-to-end serving gains.

title: Communication-Efficient Model-Distributed Inference for CBRS Radar Detection at the Edge
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Signal Processing (eess.SP)
abstract: The Citizens Broadband Radio Service (CBRS) shares the 3550-3700 MHz band between incumbent radar systems and commercial LTE/5G users, so radar activity must be detected accurately and promptly. Spectrogram-based YOLO detectors can localize coexisting radar and cellular signals, but running them on resource-constrained edge devices is challenging. Model-distributed inference (MDI) can increase throughput by partitioning a model across edge devices. Using an end-to-end pipeline from raw I/Q samples to on-device detection, we show that partitioning recent YOLO generations incurs high activation-transfer costs due to their multi-scale structures. To reduce these costs, we propose CEDAR, a communication-efficient, edge-distributed architecture for radar detection. Its RF-aware detector, CEDAR-YOLO, removes YOLO's multi-scale neck and two of its three detection scales, leaving a single-scale path with independently configured frequency and time resolutions, which lowers the communication cost of partitioning. Its compression-aware MDI framework, CEDAR-MDI, integrates lightweight activation compressors and selects, for each compressor, the partition that minimizes the pipeline bottleneck. On an NVIDIA Jetson Orin Nano testbed with real-world over-the-air data, CEDAR-YOLO reduces the parameter count by 35-57% and model inference time by 16-33%, and CEDAR-MDI achieves up to $3.27\times$ the throughput of single-device inference, with detection quality preserved in both cases.

title: When Shards Fly: Cross-Tensor In-Flight Conversion for Low-Latency, Low-Memory Weight Updates in Disaggregated RL
abstract: Disaggregated LLM reinforcement learning (RL) repeatedly synchronizes policy weights between training and rollout GPU pools. Existing systems reduce communication through shard delivery and replica forwarding, yet separate conversion passes and staging buffers still add latency and GPU-memory overheads to synchronous updates. We present ShardFly, which coordinates reusable transfer planning with streaming GPU execution for synchronous, in-place weight updates. ShardFly introduces two components. The Planner compiles native shard mappings, quantization dependencies, and replica routes into cross-tensor schedules, reserving payload buffers only for scheduled transfers. The Executor runs each rank's schedule in one persistent transfer kernel, fusing memory-layout conversion, quantization, GPU-initiated communication, and destination writes while forwarding transformed bytes across replicas. Plans and communication state are reused under stable configurations and replaced between updates for coordinated rollout scaling. On up to 32 H20 GPUs, ShardFly achieves complete BF16 weight-update speedups of 1.26--27.92$\times$ across five models and four baselines: veRL NCCL, Awex, veRL NIXL, and WeightBridge. In end-to-end Qwen3-30B-A3B GRPO across four rollout configurations, ShardFly improves response-token throughput by 5.49--6.71\% over veRL NCCL.

title: LADS: Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling of Tool Results for Language Model Agents
abstract: Web agents complete multi-step online tasks through repeated browser actions and model calls. Their returned observations lie on the critical path to subsequent decisions. When concurrent browser actions finish in bursts, observations can accumulate on a constrained return path to a shared inference service, while waiting histories compete for reusable cache state. Conventional delivery rules prioritize short transfers or immediate cache reuse but overlook how sending a result earlier can help a request resume sooner and free cache-protection capacity for other waiting requests. We present LADS (Lease-Aware Delivery Scheduling), a tool-result scheduler that couples cache-aware delivery with bounded prefix leases. Its key insight is that resumption lets extra protection references retire, making lease quota available to protect another waiting history. LADS prioritizes timely handoffs using current lease ownership and an estimated resumption delay, with bounded departures from Cache-first order. Compared with ReAct using first-in, first-out (FIFO) tool-result delivery, LADS reduces mean complete-workflow latency by 44.6% under bursty tool returns and by 42.4% on Web-derived burst replay.

title: Clockwork: Scheduling Compound AI Systems in Space Data Centers
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)
abstract: Space data centers built on LEO constellations create an opportunity to serve Compound AI workflows close to where observations are captured. Serving such a workflow for an area of interest (AoI) requires deciding which orbital planes to provision and where to place each workflow component, while orbital motion continuously changes which satellites can serve the AoI. Provisioning must therefore be planned as a sequence of decisions over time, and these decisions are coupled because changing component placements or activating new planes incurs costs. To address this, we present Clockwork, a framework for scheduling Compound AI workflows on space data centers under end-to-end latency SLOs. Clockwork has two components: i) Castor jointly selects active planes and component placements for each constellation snapshot, while ii) Pollux connects Castor's candidate provisioning states across predicted orbital evolution to construct a low-cost schedule over time. On our experimental two-shell constellation, Castor serves 81% of instances at a 300 ms SLO, while Pollux reduces mean total scheduling cost by 56% on average and by up to 63% compared to heuristic baselines.

title: Autotuning GPU Thread Block Sizes for Large-Scale Stencil Applications Using the OPS DSL
abstract: Large-scale structured-mesh stencil applications can run for hours or days on modern HPC GPU platforms, making launch-configuration choices important. OPS enables high-level stencil codes to target multiple GPU architectures, but its GPU backends rely on a default or user-selected global block/workgroup shape, even though different kernels, problem geometries, and architectures may favor different configurations. This paper presents a transparent per-kernel block/workgroup-shape autotuning extension for OPS. The extension explores valid block/workgroup shapes during execution, records the fastest configuration for each kernel, and enables precomputed replay of the selected configurations in subsequent runs. We evaluate the approach on structured-mesh proxy and academic research applications, covering 459 unique kernels across 3 NVIDIA and 2 AMD GPUs. The evaluation reports speedup distributions, representative wall-time summaries, timing variability, and input problem shape effects. Replaying the best per-kernel launch shapes improves 923 of 995 measured application/input/GPU cases over the default OPS shape. Depending on the GPU, the median speedup ranges from 1.02x to 1.18x, with individual configurations of LAPL2D, TTI3D, and OpenSBLI-based TGV solvers exceeding 1.5x. The results also show that performance sensitivity is not limited to launch shape. At fixed cell count, changing the input problem shape changes precomputed-replay runtime by 0.8-34.6% in representative cases, while kernel-level timing variability depends on the interaction between runtime contribution, input problem shape, and GPU/backend behavior. Overall, automatic per-kernel block/workgroup-shape selection improves OPS performance across GPUs, provided shape sensitivity and timing stability are interpreted together.

title: Investigating ET-SoC-1 Vector and Parallel Performance with sGEMM
abstract: The Ainekko (formerly Esperanto) ET-SoC-1 is a massively parallel RISC-V accelerator. Its compute array comprises 1024 dual-threaded in-order ET-Minion cores (2048 harts) operating at 600 MHz, each core providing an eight-lane 256-bit packed-single (PS) SIMD datapath shared by its two harts, with access to LPDDR4X memory at a nominal 133 GiB/s. This paper presents a performance investigation using single-precision general matrix multiplication (sGEMM) as the benchmark kernel. Two device kernels are implemented and evaluated on the ET-SoC-1, these are a register-blocked PS SIMD baseline with two-step software pipelining, and a TensorFMA32 kernel that drives the same FMA datapath through the per-core tensor micro-operation sequencer, with double-buffered A scratchpad loading. Because both kernels are bounded by the same arithmetic peak, the comparison isolates the effect of operand delivery from that of arithmetic width. Performance is compared against CPU references (SpacemiT K3, Intel i5-11600, AMD Ryzen 9 9950X and the Arm Cortex-X925/A725 CPU of an NVIDIA DGX Spark) and two GPUs (NVIDIA GB10 Blackwell and AMD RDNA4 RX 9060 XT).

title: Ripple: Deadline-Aware CPU-GPU Sharing for Embodied Inference
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Operating Systems (cs.OS); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: Unified-memory edge devices increasingly run LLM/VLM inference alongside time-critical CPU tasks for perception and control. GPU memory traffic can overwhelm these tasks, yet platforms such as DGX Spark expose neither bandwidth counters nor direct bandwidth regulation. We present Ripple, a CPU-GPU co-scheduler that combines model-derived GPU memory volumes with CPU completion feedback to regulate interference. Ripple divides inference into pausable, layer-based units and translates each CPU job's deadline slack into a GPU-byte budget, admitting work within the budgets of all overlapping jobs. Online updates track changing interference, while deadline-aware pacing and judicious SM footprint narrowing preserve inference progress. Implemented with SGLang engine hooks and a central scheduler, we evaluate Ripple on DGX Spark with four robotic CPU task mixes and LLM/VLM inference. It is the only evaluated approach that consistently meets the 2% CPU deadline-miss target and VLM deadlines across the tested deadline settings while retaining best-effort LLM throughput.

title: STLT: A Novel System for Energy-Aware Distributed Inference in the Edge-Cloud-Space Continuum
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
abstract: Low Earth Orbit satellites are pivotal for Earth observation tasks such as wildfire detection, capturing imagery for analysis by Deep Neural Networks (DNNs). On-board analysis reduces downlink volume, but severe energy constraints force a trade-off between computation and data transmission. Splitting the DNN between satellite and ground turns this balance into a design choice, where the split point determines combined computation and downlink energy. Existing approaches typically rely on static split-point decisions that fail to account for dynamic space conditions, or on complex algorithms, historical data, or prediction models that introduce significant overhead. To address these shortcomings, we present STLT, a two-stage system for energy-aware distributed inference between LEO satellites and a ground station. First, an offline analyzer characterizes the DNN architecture to identify a set of favorable split points, consequently reducing the search space. Second, an on-board algorithm performs lightweight energy-aware split selection, dynamically choosing from this pre-computed set based on the current state of the environment. We evaluate STLT on a real-world satellite telemetry dataset, showing that it reduces the split-candidate search space by 30.7% on average, lowers decision latency by 25.1% and energy by 27.5% on average, and delivers up to 20.1% more inference tasks than a state-of-the-art satellite-ground co-inference baseline while consuming 8.8% less energy overall.

title: Beyond Leaderless: Randomized Consensus Against Mobile Crashes
abstract: Many consensus protocols fail to terminate under attack from an adversary that has the power to move between replicas and repeatedly crash one of them, even in synchrony. We present Multi-Leader Fixed-View Simplex (ML-FVS) to defend against such an adversary while keeping the simple structure and good-case latency of Simplex consensus. Our protocol extends fixed-view Simplex with multiple leaders, each of which may broadcast a proposal. At the voting deadline, each replica votes on the set of proposals it has seen so far. A hidden threshold beacon revealed after the votes gives a priority order on the multiple leaders, resolving each vote to its highest-priority proposal. Our model combines permanent adaptive Byzantine faults with mobile crashes. For a constant crash budget and $\Delta$-delayed Byzantine corruption, we obtain $O(\Delta)$ expected latency over repeated views whose leaders start honest. With immediate Byzantine corruptions, the protocol still achieves liveness. We also evaluate the protocol under random network delays and stochastic faults, finding that multiple leaders reduce view failures even when rational leaders delay their proposals to increase rewards.

title: Token-as-a-Utility: A Model-Agnostic Architecture for Metering and Provisioning AI Inference Services
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: Token-based subscriptions are emerging as a commercial model for large language model inference, but extending them into interoperable utility services requires comparable consumption accounting. Raw token counts do not consistently measure inference resource use because demand varies with model architecture, context length, tokenisation, and concurrent serving conditions. This paper presents Token-as-a-Utility, a model-agnostic architecture integrating inference metering, service-level-aware provisioning, and inter-operator settlement. We prove that, under batched serving, no per-request meter can be additive, independent of co-resident traffic, and exactly cost-reflective at once. This motivates separating provisioned capacity, metered consumption, and contracted quality into distinct service products. Consumption is expressed in Reference Inference Units (RIUs) derived from prefill and decode demand, while occupancy-indexed operator ratings recover shared serving costs without altering the common unit. Versioned inference records support auditing and re-rating across operators; software-enforced capacity leases and quality-constrained routing enable provisioning on shared accelerators. The resource model is measured on three NVIDIA RTX 5000 Ada GPUs, and multi-tenant behaviour is evaluated with a trace-driven model calibrated to them. For the reference model, occupancy-indexed rating limits statement energy error to 9% under measured traffic, compared with up to 70.5% under fixed-occupancy rating. In calibrated multi-tenant experiments, tenant mispricing decreases from 7.36 times under flat token counting to 2.39 times with RIUs and 1.06 times after occupancy-based reconciliation. These findings demonstrate how portable inference accounting can be combined with load-dependent cost recovery and contract-based provisioning to support heterogeneous inference services across operators.

title: Layer-wise CPU-GPU Scheduling for LLM Inference on Memory-Limited Consumer GPUs
abstract: As large language model inference environments expand toward consumer devices, it remains challenging to efficiently run models that exceed GPU memory capacity in single-GPU settings. The latency of transferring weights that do not fit in GPU memory accounts for about 98\% of inference time and remains a major obstacle. In this paper, we focus on the fact that during the decode phase, layer computation time on the CPU can be shorter than weight transfer time, presenting an opportunity to hide weight transfers by utilizing this computation time. Therefore, we propose a method to hide transfer latency by executing certain layers on the CPU during the decode phase while asynchronously transferring the next layer's weights to the GPU in the background of that computation. To realize this scheduling, we formulate the placement of CPU/GPU computation and weight transfers as a latency minimization problem and perform optimization using an approximation model with relaxed temporal constraints. Evaluation results confirm that in a consumer desktop environment, our approach accelerates OPT-30B inference by 3.5x compared to HuggingFace Accelerate and 6.3x compared to DeepSpeed Zero-Inference.

title: CacheWeave: Learning to Recompute for Efficient Position-Independent KV Caching
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)
abstract: Position-independent caching reuses chunk KV caches across positions and requests. Independent encoding, however, omits cross-chunk interactions and can degrade accuracy. In our study, neither PIC training nor rule-based recomputation, alone or combined, consistently recovers full-prefill accuracy. Oracle-guided recomputation on PIC-trained models improves accuracy at the same budget, motivating better selection. We present CacheWeave, which adapts the full backbone to PIC, then freezes it and trains a model-native block selector on the adapted model's oracles. The selector uses compact cached chunk features and question hidden states without extracting backbone attention scores. It selects contiguous token blocks aligned with KV blocks to support efficient recomputation and limit copy-on-write amplification. Its runtime, CacheWeave-Serve, supports private and shared KV caches, keeps selection and recomputation on the GPU, and stages sliding-window KV for hybrid attention models. Across three models and four tasks, CacheWeave outperforms CacheBlend and ProphetKV by 7.2 and 3.5 percentage points on average at a 5% recomputation budget, with a mean relative accuracy loss of 1.6% to full prefill. With 32-token blocks, CacheWeave-Serve cuts single-request TTFT by up to 16.1x over full prefill and 1.7x over ProphetKV, and raises SLO goodput under load by up to 7.8x.

title: Computation in Anonymous Directed Dynamic Networks: Exact Worst-Case Termination Time and Network-Wise Intractability
abstract:
We determine the exact round complexity of Counting in anonymous directed dynamic networks. Agents have no identifiers, but $\ell\geq1$ of them are designated as leaders. Every agent knows $\ell$ and its own leader status, while the population size $n$ is unknown and has to be determined by the agents. Communication proceeds in synchronous rounds; the directed communication graph may change arbitrarily and unpredictably from one round to the next, but is assumed to remain strongly connected. We solve Counting with a distributed algorithm that makes every agent output $n$ and halt after a number of rounds equal to
$\begin{cases} n&\text{if }n=\ell\\ 2n-1&\text{if }n>\ell\text{ and }\ell=1\\ 2n-2&\text{if }n>\ell\text{ and }\ell\geq2. \end{cases}$
The algorithm works even for networks with loops and parallel arcs and even when agents learn their outdegree only after sending. We prove that this bound is worst-case tight over directed multigraphs for every $n$ and $\ell$ with $1\leq\ell\leq n$. Moreover, the local computation is polynomial (provided that each communication multigraph has at most $2^{\operatorname{poly}(n)}$ arcs): in every round, each agent solves at most one linear system with up to $n$ variables. By standard techniques, solving Counting also enables the evaluation of any computable function of the multiset of agents' input values within $2n-1$ communication rounds.
The bound above optimizes the worst case over all networks. For an individual network, we show that even deciding whether an agent already has enough local information to determine $n$ is $\mathsf{coNP}$-complete (provided that the numbers of parallel arcs are encoded in binary). Thus, worst-case-optimal Counting admits polynomial local computation, whereas exact network-wise optimization is intractable under standard complexity assumptions.

title: Apto: Self-Adaptive CPU-GPU Hybrid MoE Inference on Shared PCs
abstract: CPU/GPU hybrid inference enables Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models to run on memory-constrained PCs by keeping all expert weights in host memory and executing activated experts across both processors. Existing hybrid systems, however, assume exclusive resource access and determine an upfront CPU/GPU partition, so CPU contention from colocated applications can severely imbalance the two execution paths. This paper presents Apto, a self-adaptive hybrid inference system that applies dynamic scheduling to expert execution. The CPU and GPU executors claim experts from opposite ends of a dual-ended queue as they progress, allowing the CPU/GPU work split to adapt to their execution progress without predicting contention. Apto further uses affinity-aware scheduling to expose each executor's preferred experts at its queue end and cancellable tail racing to mitigate final-expert stragglers. Compared with state-of-the-art GPU-only and hybrid baselines, Apto achieves average prefill and decode speedups of 2.96$\times$ and 1.52$\times$ under standalone execution, and 5.97$\times$ and 3.45$\times$ under concurrent CPU workloads. It also accelerates real-world coding-agent applications by 2.02$\times$ on average.

title: Rethinking Model Aggregation for Federated Learning with Domain Skew: A Knowledge-Preserving Perspective
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)
abstract: Domain skew challenges federated learning by requiring a shared model to accommodate distinct visual distributions. Domain-specific experts can capture these distributions separately, creating an opportunity to integrate their representations in a unified predictor. We propose Federated Knowledge-Preserving Learning (FKPL), a two-stage framework that combines domain-oriented expert training with prototype-based classifier calibration. First, a one-shot subspace-based clustering procedure groups clients for intra-cluster training. The resulting expert encoders are concatenated and frozen, preserving each learned feature mapping during global integration. Second, clients interpolate their concatenated features with class-matched domain prototypes and upload the resulting virtual features. The server trains a global linear classifier on these features, concentrating classifier optimization at the server after a single feature upload. FKPL achieves average accuracies of 73.01\%, 67.00\%, and 64.51\% on Office-Caltech-10, PACS, and a four-domain subset of DomainNet, respectively. On DomainNet, its cross-domain standard deviation is 7.50 percentage points, the lowest among the evaluated methods. With the same concatenated extractor, prototype-based calibration improves average accuracy over federated classifier training by 9.99 and 14.94 percentage points on Office-Caltech-10 and PACS. These results identify classifier calibration as an effective way to combine preserved domain representations into a global predictor.

title: Ascend-SpMM: Accelerating Sparse Matrix-Dense Matrix Multiplication on Ascend NPUs
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Databases (cs.DB)
abstract: Sparse Matrix-Dense Matrix Multiplication (SpMM) is a fundamental kernel in graph neural networks and scientific computing, yet its optimization on Ascend NPUs remains largely unexplored. The physically decoupled Cube/Vector architecture and single-threaded scalar instruction dispatch of modern NPUs introduce unique challenges. We present Ascend-SpMM, a novel and systematic framework tailored to the physically decoupled architecture of Ascend this http URL introduce a memory-centric cost model that quantifies hardware affinity and guides a conflict-bounded, densityaware task-mapping strategy. The strategy maps dense regions to the high-throughput Cube path and sparse residuals to the flexible Vector path, with a theoretical bound on cross-processor conflicts. To execute these workloads with high efficiency, we further develop highly customized sub-kernels. These kernels leverage hierarchy-aware pipelining and round-robin ring buffer-based implicit synchronization to effectively mask memory latency and reduce instruction pipeline stalls. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Ascend-SpMM achieves a geometric-mean speedup of 12.70-20.55X over the strongest evaluated NPU baseline for each matrix, accelerates end-to-end GNN training by up to 6.8X, and delivers performance competitive with state-of-the-art GPU implementations. The source code of Ascend-SpMM is publicly available at this https URL.

title: Fairway: Load-Aware KV Cache Reuse for LLM Prefill Scheduling
abstract: LLM-based applications often employ agentic workflows and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which build long prompts from shared context. When prefixes are shared across requests, serving engines reuse the key-value (KV) cache to skip parts of the prefill computation. Reuse is typically graded: the uncached work of requests in a queue can differ by up to 100x. In this setting, the order of scheduling determines the time-to-first-token (TTFT) for the queued requests. KV reuse-first scheduling, which prioritizes the requests with the longest KV cache hit, gives the lowest median TTFT but starves expensive requests under load spikes; first-come-first-served (FCFS) scheduling bounds the tail but raises the median TTFT. We present Fairway, a prefill scheduler built on adaptive reuse prioritization: it favors KV cache reuse while queues are short, and shifts toward fair allocation as requests wait longer relative to their own prefill time. Fairway employs a virtual dual lane model: a KV reuse-first Fast lane and a Fair lane atop the serving engine's waiting queue that enables speeding up of cheap reuse requests without starving expensive ones. This model automatically adapts to the workload without any per-workload tuning. Fairway lowers the tail TTFT at no cost to the median in transient overload. Across workloads and load levels, Fairway matches or beats the best baseline, with a p99 TTFT up to 8.6x lower than prior prefix-aware schedulers. During load spikes, it keeps the tail of FCFS at a 6x lower median TTFT.

title: RegionFence: Adaptive Concurrency Control for Blockchain Parallel Transaction Execution
abstract: Smart contracts have turned blockchains into general platforms, and their throughput is increasingly limited by transaction execution. Parallel execution can relieve this bottleneck. However, most existing engines apply a single policy within a block, typically optimistic (OCC) or pessimistic (PCC) concurrency control, and thus re-execute or delay whole transactions. Although some database studies have proposed hybrid and adaptive mechanisms, these mechanisms cannot be applied directly to blockchains because the block fixes the serial order, accesses emerge only at run time, and real workloads vary widely. We propose RegionFence, an adaptive concurrency control mechanism for blockchain parallel transaction execution, based on three key designs. First, we propose regions to refine the granularity of control from whole transactions to the parts that touch contended keys. Second, we design fences to decide at run time how each region handles a conflict. Third, we introduce intra-block and inter-block online learning to anticipate likely conflicts. At the same time, the system still produces the same result as serial execution in consensus order. We implement RegionFence in go-ethereum and evaluate it on real Ethereum mainnet blocks from different periods of the past five years. Experimental results show that RegionFence achieves an overall speedup of 9.2x over single-core execution on 64 cores and outperforms OCC by 2.9-5.4x and PCC by 3.9-9.4x in speedup across these periods.

title: Exact Shortest Paths and Maximum Flow in Planar Networks in the CONGEST Model
abstract: In the CONGEST model, exact single-source shortest paths (SSSP) with nonnegative weights and exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks have both been solved in $\tilde O(D^2)$ rounds, where $D$ is the hop diameter, while the lower bound is $\Omega(D)$. Given the approximate distance labels of a recent preprint (arXiv:2606.31192), which we use as a black box, we solve exact directed SSSP in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. It rests on a lemma that answers queries from a virtual source with the labels, and on a corrected discretization of the reduction of exact to approximate distances (arXiv:2210.16351). All further bounds of the form $\tilde O(D)$ and $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ use these labels. Through the reduction of arXiv:2303.00811, SSSP with negative weights, or the detection of a negative cycle, takes $D\cdot n^{o(1)}$ rounds with high probability. We weight the face-disjoint graph of arXiv:2411.11718 so that its distances are dual distances, which turns distance problems in the dual into problems in a planar network of hop diameter $O(D)$. This gives exact maximum $st$-flow in directed planar networks in $\min\{\tilde O(D^2),D\cdot n^{o(1)}\}$ rounds with high probability, and in $\tilde O(D)$ rounds with $s,t$ on a common face. In undirected planar networks, the value of a minimum $st$-cut and a minimum cut take $\tilde O(D)$ rounds. For this we repair the auxiliary graphs of arXiv:2608.09500 at $s$ and $t$, and we show that its recursion, as we read it, can miss the minimum cut, also with exact shortest paths: on a network with $11$ vertices it reports $37$ for a minimum cut of $15$. Two more shortest-path computations per level make it exact. The virtual-source lemma, the weighting of the face-disjoint graph and the corrected discretization are machine-checked in Lean 4 with Mathlib; all other arguments are proved on paper only. Numerical checks are not used in any proof.

title: Time-Aware Urban Flood Routing with Sticky Edge Closure on Forecast Depth: A Hanoi Case Study
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Computers and Society (cs.CY)
abstract:
During urban flash floods, commuters and guiding agencies require awareness towards which roads remain passable when a vehicle actually arrives, rather than relying solely on which links appear open at initial departure. Most existing flood-routing tools apply a single static snapshot to each route; meaning that corridors that appear clear initially can become flooded before arrival. This paper presents a routing engine that ingests a two-hour water forecast, renewed every 15 minutes, and plans each journey around roads that the forecast closes for that specific vehicle class. Under this formulation, any road that closes mid-trip remains closed for that query, which keeps route calculation fast enough for live requests while operating inside a production GraphHopper routing server. Testing on a recorded storm in western Hanoi revealed that a router checking only departure conditions sent 7.8% of routes into roads flooded upon arrival. In comparable trips, the proposed rule produced longer routes in 3.95% of cases, requiring a median of only 9.2 s of additional travel time. Agencies and navigation platforms can employ this engine to schedule trips by vehicle type, allowing operators to establish depth limits and lookahead margins as policy parameters. However, several limitations must be noted, as the water depths originate from a hydrodynamic simulation that was not verified against measured water levels, the rainfall was replayed rather than forecast live, and depth cutoffs reflect policy settings rather than measured physical thresholds.
Keywords: flood routing, time-dependent shortest path, sticky edge closure, forecast water depth, vehicle depth limit, Hanoi

title: When Cache Pressure Becomes a Trap: Metastability in Agent Serving
abstract:
LLM agents repeatedly send a growing conversation to a model, making prefix reuse central to efficient serving. We show that a brief surge can disrupt this reuse and trigger metastable failure in prefill--decode (PD) disaggregated engines: service remains degraded after arrivals return to a load the engine previously sustained. On SGLang, a ten-minute surge reduced goodput by about 88% over the following hour. Removing the residual burst sessions restored service within minutes.
The sustaining mechanism is population-cache feedback. Slower calls prolong sessions and enlarge their aggregate context, or working set; the resulting cache misses increase recomputation and further delay departures. A fluid model identifies the resource conditions for this feedback and explains how cache capacity, tool time and base load affect vulnerability. Across 36 simulated deployments, it flags all 17 cache-first cases. Controlled simulations hold the post-surge state fixed and show that changing subsequent arrivals alone reverses the recovery outcome. Once the cache collapses, low-reuse departure capacity sets the scale of the load reduction needed for recovery.
Guided by these dynamics, we build Basin, which gives each session a fixed priority, reserves their predicted peak contexts against an adaptive admission budget, extends the cache with idle decode memory, and sheds excess demand. On real H200 1P3D deployments under surges, including long-context SWE-bench Pro sessions, an arrival-time prototype achieves 1.20--1.70x the goodput of Continuum and 2.35--3.59x that of HiCache alone. In simulation, the predictor-driven policy delivers 1.20--2.05x the strongest baseline's goodput across six surge scenarios.

title: OctEx: Billion-Scale Vector Search by Precomputed Lattice Neighbor Lists on GPUs
abstract: Approximate nearest-neighbor search on GPUs serves retrieval-augmented generation, recommendation, and deduplication over datasets of up to billions of vectors. The fastest GPU indexes at high recall, such as CAGRA, walk proximity graphs in chained rounds, each of which waits for the distances of the previous one. High recall therefore costs many dependent rounds per query. Our insight is to spend the HBM of the GPUs on precomputed neighbor lists, so that a query reads its candidates in one parallel step instead of a chain of rounds. This paper turns the above insight into a GPU vector search system, namely OctEx, which holds hundreds of randomly projected copies of the dataset in GPU memory. Every copy rounds its vectors to the nearest points of a regular grid whose cells are nearly round and stores for every populated cell the list of vectors nearest to its center. A query reads the lists of its cells in all copies at once and then, in a fixed number of waves, the precomputed neighbor lists of its best hits. OctEx ranks the union of all hits by an int8 sketch before one exact rerank. OctEx runs the whole search of a batch as CUDA graphs over all GPUs of a server and places every part of its index in HBM or host memory by its access frequency. On four H100 GPUs at recall 0.95 to 0.995, OctEx outperforms CAGRA by 2.0x to 46.4x on seven datasets of up to one hundred million vectors, and by 1.46x to 2.05x on the one billion vectors of Deep1B and SIFT1B, whose indexes it builds in 44 to 47 minutes. OctEx also outperforms GGNN, PathWeaver, FlowANN, and the cuVS inverted file indexes IVF-PQ and IVF-RaBitQ by 5.4x to 343x.

title: Rose: Efficient Embodied RL through Graph Optimization and GPU Compute Resource Control
abstract:
Embodied reinforcement learning (RL) coordinates policy inference, simulation, and model training with highly heterogeneous resource demands. Although individual components frequently underutilize GPU compute during execution, existing systems only overlap work at coarse component boundaries (e.g., pipelining inference and simulation across simulator groups), leaving substantial low-activity GPU windows within subcomponent phases and nested loops. Exploiting these fine-grained windows manually requires tedious dependency analysis and workload-specific coordination. Furthermore, even when independent work is scheduled concurrently, cross-process GPU time slicing and streaming multiprocessor (SM) contention can negate the benefits of overlap.
We present Rose, a runtime-aware system that automates fine-grained overlap and GPU resource management for embodied RL while preserving synchronous training semantics. Through a lightweight programmable interface that exposes execution hierarchy and state accesses, Rose tracks runtime data readiness and GPU activity to perform a two-stage optimization. First, a window-guided graph optimizer identifies low-activity windows and applies graph transformations to overlap complementary work across components and loop levels. Second, leveraging NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) for cross-process GPU concurrency, a slack-aware resource manager tunes process-level SM quotas by exploiting branch synchronization slack to mitigate interference on the critical path. Both stages combine local profiling with end-to-end iteration validation to guarantee throughput gains with minimal tuning overhead. Across diverse policies, simulators, RL algorithms, and GPU platforms, Rose achieves 1.20--1.92$\times$ training throughput improvement and increases average SM activity by 23.8--39.3\% compared with the state-of-the-art systems.

title: Local Zero-Shot Latency Prediction for Low-End GPUs
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: Quantifying execution latency is an important consideration across Machine Learning. Existing latency-prediction approaches typically train ML models on traces collected from workload execution on target hardware. Collection of representative traces across many consumer GPUs is expensive both in organizing the devices and in manpower, causing existing work to mainly focus on a limited set of high-end GPUs available in cloud computing. To offset this cost, we show that a local host GPU can be configured to reproduce the execution performance of less powerful target GPUs. Through selectively modifying device parameters, we obtain locally measured latencies that closely approximate those observed on the target hardware. We reformulate the latency-prediction task: instead of fitting a prediction model to a dataset of execution traces, we identify local configurations that best reproduce target devices' performance, enabling zero-shot prediction. We evaluate our approach against real measurements from 60 computer-vision models executed on 21 consumer GPU models. Our method achieves a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of 14.21%, compared with more than 25% for comparable baselines, reducing relative prediction error by 43.6%. Predicted and measured latencies exhibit an average Spearman correlation of 0.961 across training tasks, demonstrating that the method also accurately preserves performance rankings across devices.

title: Dispatch Control for Priority-Based, Multi-Tenant Workflows under Multi-Resource External Rate Limits
abstract: Workflow engines orchestrate pipelines of activities, which often call external APIs, on a fixed pool of worker slots, the threads that run them. When an API enforces a hard rate limit shared by all tenants and priorities, a throttled call that retries after a backoff keeps its worker slot and starves other tenants. Large Language Model provider APIs are particularly complex: their per-organization caps are low and bind independently on requests and tokens per minute. The operator can neither reconfigure the cap nor observe saturation before a request fails, so classical fair-queuing assumptions do not hold. We present Backpressure, a worker-side admission gate. It checks each call's cost atomically against shared admission state and enforces fairness over requests and tokens. A denied call releases its worker slot and waits on a durable timer, so waiting no longer blocks execution capacity. We compare against a naive retry, the AI gateway LiteLLM, and the built-in throttle of the workflow engine Temporal. On a workload with three priority classes, Backpressure raises fairness (Jain's index over each queue's fraction of its entitled share) from 0.60 to 0.89, where 1.0 is ideal. It also cuts high-priority tail latency roughly 8x. When tokens are the binding limit, all request-based baselines serve every priority equally, whereas Backpressure keeps the priority order and reaches a dominant-resource fairness of ~0.99. Admission costs one round trip to shared state, adds no measurable latency when the cap does not bind, and fails open if shared state is unavailable.

title: Introducing Cluster Efficiency to LLM Serving: Pooling Economical Accelerators over Fast Interconnects
abstract: Long-context large language model (LLM) serving places substantial demands on compute, memory capacity, and memory bandwidth. Economical accelerators can offer these resources at lower cost, but their limited per-device capacity requires pooling across devices, making communication overhead critical. We study cluster efficiency, measured in tokens per dollar and per joule, and show how low-latency, high-bandwidth interconnects enable economical accelerators to retain their cost advantage. Guided by a characterization of coding-agent workloads and accelerator scaling, we realize this design on the Tenstorrent Galaxy, a cluster of Blackhole chips. The serving stack combines integrated communication engines, pipelined ring transfers, communication-computation overlap, and device-side decode replay to reduce collective overhead. Across three dense models in BF16 and 8-bit configurations with 8K-256K-token contexts, the Galaxy achieves 1.07-2.24$\times$ the tokens per dollar of an eight-GPU RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell server under a three-year acquisition-and-electricity cost model. Emulating TCP-class communication on the same chips reduces throughput by 23.5-67.4% and eliminates the cost advantage in every evaluated configuration. These results demonstrate how fast interconnects translate the per-dollar resource advantages of economical accelerators into cost-efficient long-context LLM serving.

title: Same Function, Different CPU: Quantifying Hardware Heterogeneity in Commercial FaaS Platforms
abstract:
Serverless computing, particularly Function-as-a-Service (FaaS), abstracts operational concerns such as scaling, scheduling, and resource management from users. This abstraction, however, conceals a heterogeneous hardware fleet on which function execution environments are scheduled behind a unified function interface. Consequently, otherwise identical invocations may run on different CPU types that differ in performance, a hardware lottery that users can neither see nor control. Since the resulting variability is entangled with other sources, such as noisy neighbors or diurnal effects, its contribution to overall performance variability and how this contribution differs across providers remain unclear.
In this paper, we systematically study hardware heterogeneity and its impact on function performance across four widely used commercial FaaS platforms, covering regional, configurational, and temporal differences. Using variance decomposition, we find that CPU heterogeneity alone explains 4 % to 97 % of the performance variance on AWS Lambda and Google Cloud Run Functions. On Azure Functions, in contrast, we identify a platform-level mechanism that produces bimodal execution durations and overshadows CPU effects. We observe that the CPU composition on AWS Lambda shifts within a single week. Additionally, we reveal that on Google Cloud Run Functions and Alibaba Function Compute, the availability of instruction set extensions such as SHA-NI differs between CPU types, widening the performance gap further. Since all platforms bill by duration, performance gaps between CPU types translate directly into cost, with invocations on the slowest CPU type costing up to three times as much as those on the fastest.

title: DynSL: Resource-Adaptive Model Training across Heterogeneous Edge Devices
subjects: Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Networking and Internet Architecture (cs.NI)
abstract: Training models over data distributed across edge devices presents a trade-off: centralizing data simplifies training but raises privacy and regulatory concerns, while full local training may exceed the devices' compute and memory capacity. Split learning addresses this challenge by partitioning the model between clients and the server, allowing part of the computation to be offloaded. However, existing approaches typically rely on static split configurations or simplified assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneity and complex dynamics of real deployments. We present DynSL, a framework that dynamically allocates model layers between clients and the server by continuously monitoring system metrics and periodically solving an optimization problem that accounts for client and server computation and communication. When beneficial, the system reconfigures the split, enabling the offloading strategy to adapt to changing device capabilities and system conditions. Extensive experiments on a testbed of 24 heterogeneous edge devices show that DynSL reduces training time by up to $\sim\!$30% over the strongest adaptive baseline and by more than 50% over a suboptimal uniform split, with no loss -- and sometimes a gain -- in accuracy.

title: Robustness Starts with the Objective: Designing and Certifying Robust LLM-Generated Heuristics
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract:
LLMs are increasingly used to design heuristics for computer systems. However, most synthesis frameworks evaluate candidates by their average performance, which can mask severe regressions on specific workloads. Even adding adversarial training inputs doesn't eliminate these regressions, and percentile objectives (e.g., optimizing for the 95th percentile) overlook how severe regressions can be beyond the selected threshold.
We present TAILOR, a framework that guides LLM synthesis using the Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR) of the cost difference between each candidate and an existing baseline on the same workload. This paired CVaR measures the average difference over the worst fraction of workloads. We show that a negative paired CVaR guarantees improvements in both average performance and tail optimality gap relative to the unknown optimum, without ever computing that optimum.
We find that TAILOR achieves the best mean--tail trade-off among the synthesis objectives we evaluate across three case studies: Azure GPU batch admission, Azure VM packing, and server placement. Tested across seven diverse optimization benchmarks, TAILOR produces heuristics that are certified with 99% confidence to improve both average performance and tail optimality gaps over the baseline in six of them. On these six benchmarks, TAILOR also outperforms known robust, human-designed alternatives in the tail while achieving better or comparable average-performance improvement over the baseline.

title: Running a 20B Video Diffusion Transformer on Consumer Hardware: A Deployment and Measurement Report for MiniMax H3 on Apple Silicon
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: We report the end-to-end deployment and measurement of MiniMax H3, a 20.38-billion-parameter video diffusion transformer (DiT) - the count measured from the safetensors headers of the Q8 checkpoint as deployed locally (Section 3.2) - running entirely on consumer Apple Silicon hardware: an Apple Mac mini with M5 Pro chip and 64 GiB of unified memory. Using the official bf16-to-Q8 (8-bit, group size 64) quantization path executed locally on the machine, we produced a working text-to-video pipeline with no cloud dependency. We document the full deployment procedure, including two non-trivial blockers and their fixes, and report measured figures for build time, peak memory, and per-clip render latency across four resolution tiers (Draft 384x640 through Native 768x1344). A 15.08-second 576x1024 clip rendered in 4838.49 seconds with a measured MLX peak of 27.467 GiB. We further operated the system as an unattended production pipeline, completing 17 clips in 26.49 hours with zero render failures. A blind human review of the 17 production clips (generation prompts withheld) averaged 3.12, 3.18, and 2.94 out of 5 for structural integrity, temporal consistency, and visible artifacts. All figures in this report are our own measurements except where explicitly labeled as third-party data. This is a systems/empirical report; we make no claim of model innovation.

title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

title: Multi-Turn Semantic Caching for Low-Cost LLM Serving
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Semantic caching lowers the cost of serving large language models (LLMs) by reusing stored responses for similar requests. In multi-turn conversations, whether a cached response is acceptable depends on both conversations' histories, which embedding similarity of requests and histories predicts poorly (AUC 0.62--0.74 on five workloads). We therefore learn the \emph{reuse risk}, the probability that a cached response is unacceptable, from judge feedback, and choose a budgeted set of conversation states to cache by weighing the generation cost a reuse avoids against a price for unacceptable reuse. We propose CUCB-SC-MT, which learns a cache from logged conversations with a suboptimality guarantee, and CLCB-LS-MT, which learns online and has $\tilde O(\sqrt N)$ regret over $N$ requests when conversation states recur. On math-tutoring (SocraTeach) and movie-ticketing (Taskmaster-3) conversations, both achieve lower loss than prior semantic caching approaches: ContextCache, multi-turn variants of ElastiCache and vCache, and single-turn semantic caching at every cache budget. With 1,000 cache entries, CLCB-LS-MT avoids 35--41\% of the generation cost through acceptable reuses, against at most 22--25\% for the baselines, and lowers estimated serving latency by 19--35\%.

title: CuPH: Parallel Cubical Persistent Homology via Level-Synchronous Component Tracking
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Computational Geometry (cs.CG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Persistent homology (PH) is a mathematically principled multi-scale topological descriptor of shape and connectivity in data. It is widely applied in image classification, segmentation, and shape analysis across medical and aerial imaging, providing structural information that pixel-wise deep learning may overlook. Standard cubical PH decomposes an image into cubical cells (vertices, edges, and squares) and reduces them sequentially in filtration order. This sequential reduction has $\Theta(n)$ parallel depth for an $n$-pixel image, limiting within-image GPU parallelism and constraining its use in topology-aware deep learning. We introduce CuPH, a GPU-based parallel algorithm for computing cubical PH on 2D images that operates directly on pixels rather than cubical cells. CuPH buckets pixels by filtration values, activates them with a level-synchronous sweep, and tracks connected components with a lock-free union-find method. We prove that CuPH produces persistence diagrams identical to standard cubical PH on integer inputs, with a stability bound for floating-point inputs. CuPH reduces parallel depth from $\Theta(n)$ to $O(L\log n)$ for an image with $L$ intensity levels. We implement the level sweep as a single CUDA kernel, eliminating cross-level kernel-launch overhead. Empirically, CuPH is $18.6$--$99.6\times$ faster than the existing GPU baseline (CMP). As a drop-in PH backend, CuPH accelerates topology-aware classification ($4.2$--$16.7\times$) and segmentation ($8.3$--$44\times$) while preserving accuracy. It also enables computing full-image PH losses on high-resolution images, improving segmentation Dice by $2.2$--$4.6$ points over patch-local PH baselines and accelerating training by $25$--$31\times$.

title: Fast and Exact Relative-Position Attention via Structure-Aware Kernels
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Relative-position attention mechanisms offer compelling alternatives to RoPE across various transformer architectures, delivering superior performance in domains such as audio. These mechanisms typically modify attention scores by adding content-position or bias-position terms. Unlike RoPE, which encodes position via per-token rotations directly on the queries and keys, relative-position terms generally require pairwise offset-dependent computation or lookups, complicating their integration into fused attention kernels and introducing severe memory, bandwidth, and compute overheads as sequences scale. To address this bottleneck, we propose an exact attention algorithm that incorporates additive relative-position terms into FlashAttention-style tiled computation. Our method (1) uses offset-aware tiling to avoid redundant indexing and memory accesses, (2) computes only the necessary key/query-relation products and reuses them across token pairs in both forward and backward passes, and (3) uses offset-based gradient sharding and aggregation, eliminating atomic contention. We provide a unified, efficient Triton implementation across diverse relative-position attention mechanisms and evaluate it against naive and specialized implementations. For 8K-token sequences, our method speeds up the forward (backward) pass by 1.8-6.4$\times$ (2.0-21$\times$) and reduces peak memory up to 2.9-128$\times$ (1.4-54$\times$) over the strongest baseline for each mechanism, enabling long-context end-to-end transcription that is 1.8$\times$ faster and uses 2.4$\times$ less memory. Our method thus provides a drop-in, hardware-efficient solution for scaling relative-position attention transformers.

title: AdapBench: Adaptive Early-Stopping and Prioritization for Efficient Microbenchmarking in Cloud-based CI/CD
subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Performance (cs.PF)
abstract: Cloud-based software systems frequently release new versions, a fact further accelerated through agentic coding. Each new release, however, brings the risk of performance regressions which can irritate end users, increase infrastructure costs, and increase carbon footprints. Therefore, developers strive to catch such regressions in testing stages, usually through so-called continuous benchmarking. The standard way of doing this is using microbenchmark suites which, however, take notoriously long to execute. Optimizing the execution of microbenchmark suites is, hence, an active field of research. In this paper, we propose AdapBench, an online scheduling system for reducing the execution duration of microbenchmark suites. AdapBench is the first approach which dynamically makes at-runtime decisions for prioritizing the most informative benchmarks and early-stopping each one once enough evidence has accumulated to accept or reject a performance change hypothesis. We evaluate our prototype on eight popular Java projects, commonly used by microbenchmark research, and four additional Go projects. At matched 90% change detections and false-positive rate compared to an optimistic uniform run, AdapBench saves 42% of the aggregate execution duration on the Java projects, with negligible scheduling overhead (below 0.001% of the total runtime). On the Go projects, AdapBench finds every performance change with zero false positives while saving 85% of the full run.

title: Eliminating Servers in State Machine Replication
subjects: Databases (cs.DB); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: State Machine Replication (SMR) underpins many stateful systems, including distributed databases, coordination services, and metadata stores. Fundamentally, SMR requires state to be materialized from a durable total order of commands. Existing SMR systems rely on servers to materialize, locally store, and serve snapshots of state; while the durable total order either resides on the same servers, or on an external, disaggregated shared log. Unfortunately, servers act as brittle, expensive choke-points in such systems, causing service unavailability when they fail; incurring provisioning latency on cold starts; and red-lining when exposed to bad clients. In this paper, we propose Serverless SMR (S^2MR), where both the materialized state and the durable total order are stored on disaggregated storage; clients concurrently maintain a single copy of materialized state on external storage. Our key technical insight is that the shared log abstraction is useful not just for consistently ordering commands in SMR, but also for enabling distributed materialization, thus becoming the only interface for ac hieving SMR. We demonstrate S^2MR by developing AirDB, a transactional key-value store. In our evaluation, AirD B over S^2MR achieves higher availability than existing SMR-based systems like etcd over Raft: it is oblivious to server failures and bad client activity; and spins up 10x-45x faster from a cold start.

title: Serving Agentic Robot Fleets: Workload Characterization, KV-Cache Thrashing, and Admission Control
subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Agentic robots combine a vision-language brain, a tool-using harness, and a vision-language-action (VLA) policy. Serving a fleet of these agents introduces two coupled resource constraints: the brain repeatedly revisits long, growing key-value (KV) cache states, while the VLA executes action chunks under tight control deadlines. We characterize 80 LIBERO-PRO episodes generated by GPT-6-Astra, RPent, and pi0.5 (1,862 brain turns and 1,582 VLA inference chunks), profile both layers on H800 graphics processing units (GPUs), and replay the resulting agent programs on a vLLM serving engine. Brain contexts reach 215k tokens; the median Astra request takes 7.78 s, while the intervening environment-step gap is only 1.0 s. Under a 0.25 s action-chunk deadline, one VLA GPU meets the 1% starvation target for one robot; under a 1.0 s deadline, its measured capacity reaches at least 32. In sustained brain replay, increasing concurrency from 20 to 32 robots reduces throughput from about 2.4 to 0.6 requests/s as repetitive prefill displaces generation. A static active-episode cap restores 2.24-2.25 requests/s and raises completed trace-program throughput from 1.30 to 5.00-5.55 episodes/min. Our measurements expose the workload-dependent shift between action deadlines and brain KV residency, and establish practical principles for capacity planning and admission in sustained agentic robot fleets.

title: DIMWIT: Directly Invoking Models Without Intensive Tuning
subjects: Performance (cs.PF); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Operating Systems (cs.OS)
abstract: Resource managers typically encode what to do in a task-specific policy---a heuristic, an optimization procedure, or a model trained for the task---that must be developed before use and may need revision as the workload or system changes. We propose bypassing policy development and instead asking pretrained models to make resource-management decisions directly, given the current system state, desired outcome, and available choices. We evaluate this approach on microservice autoscaling, DRAM sizing, and video encoding, using a frontier LLM and two small decision models. On two microservice applications, a small decision model meets latency targets while using within 10% of the replicas allocated by policy-based autoscalers and within 13% of the frontier LLM. In DRAM sizing, a small decision model reduces DRAM usage by up to 27.5% relative to static provisioning while maintaining at least 95% of baseline performance. In video encoding, it completes encodes up to 4.3$\times$ faster than the frontier LLM, with an imperceptible 1.1-point decrease in Video Multi-Method Assessment Fusion (VMAF), a metric of perceptual video quality. Making individual resource-management decisions may be considerably simpler than developing a general strategy for making them.

title: A Compute Center Anyone Can Join: A Peer-to-Peer System for AI Inference
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT)
abstract: Today, most people obtain AI inference by buying it from a small number of organizations that run large data centers, while many GPUs owned by individuals and small institutions sit idle for much of the day. Bitcoin showed that strangers can contribute resources under shared rules and receive checkable rewards, but it relies on an asymmetry: proof-of-work is expensive to produce and cheap to verify. Useful inference has no such asymmetry. We propose the Open Inference Market (OIM), which replaces the missing asymmetry with an economic mechanism. A worker delivers a result without knowing whether it will be audited; its unsettled earnings serve as collateral during a challenge window; and confirmed cheating forfeits all of it. We call this principle earnings as collateral. In a simplified model we show three things. The number of audits needed for deterrence is a constant per worker per day, independent of the worker's throughput, so the audited share falls as the network gets busier. A new worker can join with a short period of intensive auditing and a very small bond. And whether the mechanism works at all depends only on the ratio of the audit judge's false-flag rate to its detection rate. Under example parameters, about 0.3 replays per worker per day are enough to make cheating unprofitable for a rational worker. On this basis we lay out a path that hands four powers back to participants one at a time: owning compute, writing history, judging work, and releasing value. A compute center need not be a building; it can be a protocol that anyone can join.

title: Superscalar Loop Processors
subjects: Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: To sustain the computational demands of modern ML and HPC workloads, programmable accelerators integrate large arrays of processing elements (PEs), typically built around single-issue in-order cores to maximize integration density and energy efficiency. As a result, each PE's instruction throughput is upper-bounded at one instruction per cycle (IPC), often suffering from significant underutilization of its functional units (FUs). Conventional superscalar processors can improve FU utilization by increasing IPC, but they typically incur substantial area and energy overheads. This work proposes the Superscalar Loop Processor (SLP) architecture, a lightweight approach to superscalar execution that targets regular, compute-intensive loop kernels. We present the SLP execution model, which exploits the static structure of these workloads to enable efficient multiple-issue execution without the complexity of dynamic out-of-order scheduling. We demonstrate the SLP architecture through an open-source prototype implementation, Schnizo, developed as an enhancement of a tiny RV32I core with floating-point support. Across several ML and HPC microkernels, Schnizo achieves substantially higher IPC and FPU utilization than the scalar baseline while retaining the efficiency of lightweight in-order designs. These results demonstrate that SLPs can provide an efficient architectural solution for programmable accelerators targeting regular, compute-intensive workloads.

title: ReWY: Faster Gradient Computation for Delta-Rule Attention Family
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract:
Delta-rule linear attention underlies language models such as Kimi Linear and Qwen3-Next. Chunkwise implementations expose matrix parallelism, but their backward passes compute unnecessary auxiliary adjoints. We present ReWY, an algebraic reformulation that reduces this work before optimizing accelerator execution. Differentiating the chunk correction as one triangular residual system eliminates the inverse adjoint and reduces seven local WY matrix products to three. Two complementary transformations expose further reuse: centered matrix contractions replace pairwise vector-gate processing, and scalar-gate reductions reuse key-gradient products instead of forming a key Gram matrix. These identities simplify backward computation for DeltaNet, GDN, KDA, and GDN2 while preserving the recurrence and gradients in exact arithmetic, without changing the architecture or training objective.
We implement the reduced graph on GPUs and Ascend NPUs. Under matched recomputation and full-saving policies, precision-qualified six-shape comparisons with frozen FLA references yield 1.15-1.81$\times$ geometric-mean complete low-level backward speedups on NVIDIA GPUs. All four operators achieve 1.18-1.70$\times$ on H100 and H200 while retaining original FP32 working matrices. A separate public-autograd evaluation on Ascend 950DT, including gradient conversions, yields 1.09-2.89$\times$ under available matched policies. Paired ablations establish further ReWY gains after optimizing the complementary contractions. Complete-gradient checks validate the recorded operator cases; supplementary full-model backward measurements assess integration into community FLA models and a GDN2 layer port. Code and reproduction materials: this https URL.

title: Paying for Fractional Error: Tight Constant-Round Approximation of Covering Problems with Short Broadcasts
subjects: Data Structures and Algorithms (cs.DS); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract:
We present a general framework for deterministic constant-round approximation of covering problems in sparse networks in the broadcast CONGEST model, where every vertex broadcasts the same $O(\log n)$-bit message to all its neighbors. The framework combines two independent tools. The first is a solver that computes a $(1+\delta)$-approximate solution of any local covering linear program with bounded positive integer costs on every class that excludes a fixed minor. The second is a rounding principle: a rounding rule that saves a fixed fraction of its own output, for every feasible input, pays for a solver error fixed in advance, so that an approximate fractional solution yields an exact coefficient.
For ordinary domination, we achieve a $2a+1$ approximation against the fractional optimum $\gamma_f(G)$ for every fixed rational $a\ge1$, whenever every minor has a ratio of edges to vertices of at most $a$. On planar graphs this is seven, matching the lower bound of Hilke, Lenzen, and Suomela. The coefficients are also optimal at bounded treewidth and pathwidth, for $K_t$-minor-free graphs with $3\le t\le9$, on triangle-free planar graphs (five), and on planar graphs of large girth, where it approaches the optimal three. On every fixed surface the exact bound is $7\gamma(G)$, and we show that a bound of $7\gamma_f(G)$ is impossible on some fixed surfaces even sequentially.
For total domination, on graphs without isolated vertices and under the same minor-density assumption, the exact coefficient is $2a$ against the fractional optimum, including the optimal six on planar graphs. Red-blue domination, and hence set cover and hitting set on planar incidence graphs, has the optimal limiting coefficient four. Our method also gives randomized constant-round and deterministic $O(\log^* n)$-round $(1+\varepsilon)$-approximation schemes, with the randomized cost guarantee holding in expectation.

title: Conditional Calibration Contracts under Coupled Load: A Branch-Aware Audit of Switched Inference
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Bursty serving changes both queue states and the population selected for each model. We study conditional calibration contracts as a specification to be validated, rather than a certified property of an existing router. CA-MHD combines load-coupled distillation, closed-loop replay and a cost-informed Schmitt router in a discrete-event simulator with a hardware service table. Across 40 cells (ten training seeds and four content-load coupling levels), we distinguish the original teacher, frozen wide heads on an adapted trunk, and the narrow student. A common teacher-trajectory audit has median absolute student-teacher deficit 0.06 percentage points, but does not certify the student-selected deployment support. Historical results use a kernel correctness gap, not the published SmoothECE; we separately prove selected-branch composition for a residual functional at a common fixed scale. The deployed wide branch has lower ordinal accuracy than the original teacher in all 40 cells. Same-checkpoint student-only serving has lower historical ordinal gap in 27/40 cells; routing also exposes violation tails up to 17.5 percent. Student p99 latency remains above the 1.5 ms target. Retrospective temporal recalibration improves the ordinal gap in 39/40 cells, but causal delayed-label availability is unverified and no incremental per-mode benefit is detected after multiplicity adjustment. An in-sample CUSUM detects 30/40 checkpoint changes at five historical false alarms, with no prospective false-alarm guarantee. These findings support a branch-aware audit and a scoped negative result, not demonstrated routing superiority. Independent budgets, selected-support validation and net utility under a satisfied SLA remain open.

title: Turbo-GMM: FlashAttention-Inspired GPU-Accelerated Gaussian Mixture Model
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC)
abstract: Expectation-maximization (EM) for Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) requires scoring $N$ data points against $K$ mixture components. Prior fused GPU implementations, notably Flash-GMM, eliminate materialization of the $N \times K$ responsibility matrix but traverse the component dimension twice to compute normalization terms and accumulate sufficient statistics. We introduce Turbo-GMM, a single-sweep fused EM kernel that completes responsibility normalization and sufficient-statistic accumulation within one traversal of the component dimension. By retaining the complete component axis on chip, Turbo-GMM avoids the second score computation required by the released two-sweep Flash-GMM implementation. Its applicability is limited by register pressure, occupancy, and the component and feature dimensions, making it particularly suitable for large datasets with relatively small numbers of components. For larger configurations, Turbo-GMM employs a two-pass fallback following the established fused design. We establish algebraic equivalence to standard EM in real arithmetic and evaluate sixteen configurations on an NVIDIA A100. Under the reported benchmarking protocol, Turbo-GMM achieves a median $2.15\times$ speedup over the evaluated Flash-GMM implementation and up to $5.3\times$ and $9.9\times$ over PyTorch and \texttt{scikit-learn}, respectively. The results demonstrate the potential of single-sweep component traversal while identifying on-chip resource constraints as the principal limitation of this approach.

title: TLAPS-Bench: Formally Proving Correctness of Real-World System Specifications with TLA+ Proof System
subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Logic in Computer Science (cs.LO); Software Engineering (cs.SE)
abstract: TLAPS-Bench is a benchmark and execution harness for constructing machine-checked proofs for real-world system specifications in TLA+ with agentic AI. Proving correctness of complex system specifications requires discovering inductive invariants, reasoning about intricate state transitions, and decomposing proofs into tractable obligations. TLAPS-Bench provides a proof harness that supports iterative proof development atop the TLA+ Proof System (TLAPS), where agents are equipped with proof tools and libraries, with safeguards against reward hacking. Using the harness, we have employed AI agents to prove desired properties for important system specifications that were not proved before, spanning cache coherence, Byzantine consensus, and write-ahead logs. TLAPS-Bench contains 265 proof targets (each encodes a property to prove) from 95 TLA+ specifications of real-world systems. We evaluated frontier AI agents, represented by Codex with GPT models, on a subset of 70 proof targets across 12 specifications.
