First, the per-pixel depth search disregards semantic similarity within the 2D feature space, causing depth search operations to account for over 65% of memory traffic due to redundant exhaustive candidate scans. Second, the sequential pipeline of depth prediction followed by Gaussian generation neglects local 3D geometric continuity, resulting in more than 52% of generated Gaussians being redundant prior to instantiation. In this paper, we introduce SCARF, a dataflow-co-designed accelerator that aligns each bottleneck with a corresponding scene-level regularity. To mitigate the first bottleneck, Feature Similarity Depth Reuse reconceptualizes depth search as a problem of semantic locality: depth consistency is determined by affinity in feature space rather than physical address proximity. It transforms exhaustive per-pixel depth searches into anchor-centered local searches. To overcome the second bottleneck, Scene-Adaptive Early Sparsification disrupts the conventional serial depth-to-materialization boundary by probing each tile to infer local scene regularity. It then selectively activates only the minimally sufficient generation pathway, eliminating redundant Gaussian computations before primitive instantiation. On a 27.8 square millimeter 28 nm post-layout design, SCARF delivers a 2.94x geometric-mean end-to-end speedup with maximum PSNR degradation below 0.072%, 2.23 inferences per joule, and 34.5x GPU energy efficiency.

title: Malware Clustering in the Wild: Taxonomy, Challenges, and Evaluation Metrics
abstract: As malware continues to grow in volume, diversity, and sophistication, clustering has emerged as a critical technique for analyzing large malware corpora. Clustering enables the discovery of structural relationships, behavioral patterns, and evolutionary trends, and is widely used to group unknown samples, infer malware family boundaries, and identify novel variants. However, existing research remains fragmented, employing a wide range of clustering techniques with no unified perspective that systematically organizes prior work or clearly identifies gaps in the literature. This survey addresses this gap by organizing previous malware clustering research into seven categories: centroid-based, hierarchical-based, density-based, distribution-based, mixed- type, fuzzy, and AI-driven approaches. In addition, this survey summarizes publicly available malware datasets commonly used in clustering research and examines the feature representations derived from these datasets. Our goal is to clarify the current landscape and outline promising avenues for future research on malware clustering, including how AI-driven methods may shape large-scale and reproducible analysis.

title: Discovering Semantic Granularity in Images through Clustering of Pretrained Visual Representations
abstract: Semantic granularity, which refers to the levels at which visual representations organize image content into meaningful entities, is fundamental to image understanding. However, whether pretrained visual representations inherently encode semantic structures at multiple granularities remains poorly understood. This paper presents a representation-driven approach for discovering semantically meaningful image regions at different granularities through clustering of pretrained visual representations without semantic supervision. Specifically, we concatenate selected feature maps extracted from a pretrained visual model and apply a singular value decomposition (SVD)-based projection to derive pixel-wise principal representation maps (PRMs). The resulting PRMs capture implicit semantic structures embedded in pretrained visual representations, making them accessible to subsequent semantic clustering. We then introduce the semantic continuity rate (SCR), based on the silhouette principle, to quantify the coherence of pixel-wise representations within and between clusters at different candidate granularities. Furthermore, we analyze the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of SCR profiles to assess representation suitability for discovering semantic regions at multiple granularities. Our results indicate that PRMs exhibiting higher SNR values over an initial range of cluster numbers tend to yield more semantically meaningful regions across multiple granularities. We evaluate the proposed approach on the COCO-2017 and VOC-2012 validation datasets using Hungarian-matched intersection over union (HIoU). The results demonstrate competitive segmentation performance among the compared methods, supporting the feasibility of discovering useful semantic granularities through clustering PRMs without semantic supervision.

title: Efficient Detailed Scheduling of Multiproduct Pipelines using Action-Decoupled Deep Reinforcement Learning
subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Systems and Control (eess.SY); Optimization and Control (math.OC)
abstract: Multiproduct pipelines transport refined products to delivery stations in sequential batches, and their detailed scheduling must meet market demand while respecting nonlinear hydraulic constraints. Retaining the full hydraulic nonlinearity yields a mixed-integer nonlinear program that is computationally intractable, while the linearization commonly adopted for solver-based optimization degrades hydraulic accuracy without resolving the heavy computational burden. This paper develops an action-decoupled proximal policy optimization (PPO) framework that efficiently produces detailed schedules while preserving hydraulic fidelity. The scheduling process is cast as a semi-Markov decision process (SMDP) with flexible action durations. To handle the discrete-continuous hybrid action space, a cascaded dual-actor architecture decouples the discrete operating duration from the continuous flow decisions, eliminating the gradient interference that destabilizes conventional coupled-action policies and thereby yielding high-quality schedules far more efficiently. Validated on a real-world multiproduct pipeline in China and benchmarked against a single-actor baseline and a linearized MILP solved by Gurobi, the proposed framework achieves delivery accuracy close to the exact optimum while substantially improving flow rate stability and substantially reducing solution time.

title: Window-Aware Scheduling for Health Messaging under Platform Delivery Constraints: Evidence from an AI-Powered WhatsApp Maternal and Infant Health Chatbot in Nigeria
subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Computers and Society (cs.CY)
abstract: WhatsApp lets a business send free-form messages only within 24 hours of a user's last message; outside this customer service window, only pre-approved templates are delivered. Health chatbots inherit this rule, but its cost is rarely measured. We analyse 98,607 messages sent to 3,696 mothers by a WhatsApp maternal health chatbot in Nigeria, with a largely separate export as replication. No free-form message failed with the window open (0 of 35,500), and failure jumped by 93.0 percentage points (95% CI 87.0 to 99.1) at exactly 24 hours. Two flows produced 66.1% of failures, including an offer to speak with a medical professional that, as built, reached 0.3 in 100 mothers whose window had closed. We formalise window-aware scheduling as a decision problem with an action of known zero value. Model-based offline evaluation, with bounds for unconfirmed delivery, estimates that sending the offer as an approved template would reach 81.5 to 86.8 in 100 such mothers, against 16.6 for waiting and 11.6 for a reply prompt. In a calibrated simulation, tabular Q-learning converges to the same template rule and does not beat it in any of 13 stress tests, and opting out does not rise with message volume. The main gain comes from respecting the platform rule, and it needs no learning. All outcomes are deliveries, not health outcomes.

title: GPU-Native Real-Time Textured Mesh Reconstruction with Seam-Aware Multi-View Radiometric Correction
subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Graphics (cs.GR)
abstract: We present a GPU-native volumetric-video system for real-time reconstruction of graphics-compatible textured triangle meshes from multiple RGB-D sensors. Existing TSDF systems accelerate fusion and mesh extraction, but extending them to per-frame textured meshing adds CPU mesh processing, CPU-side texturing work, or extra CPU-GPU transfers between stages. After input staging, our method keeps the reconstruction and texturing stages (TSDF fusion, Marching Cubes, connected-component noise removal, view-based texture mapping, inpainting, and radiometric seam correction) resident on the GPU; no intermediate mesh or image data returns to the host between these stages. A fixed-size-array representation of mesh topology gives constant-time neighbor access on the GPU and makes the downstream mesh-level operations data-parallel. Because we texture each face from a single camera, exposure seams that vary smoothly across each image remain; we estimate a per-camera low-frequency gain field and bake it into the atlas on the GPU. On the CMU Panoptic dataset, our method is faster than the baselines at every tested voxel resolution and number of sensors, achieves peak speedups of more than an order of magnitude over CUDA-accelerated nvblox and CPU-based Open3D, and approaches an offline textured-meshing baseline in perceptual re-rendering quality.

title: Exact Sum-of-Radii Clustering under Any Constant Stability
abstract:
We establish a separation between the stability thresholds of Minimum Sum-of-Radii (MSR) clustering and two closely related objectives. Known hardness results show that, on general metrics, exact recovery for Minimum Sum-of-Diameters and symmetric $k$-center is hard for every fixed $1<\gamma<2$, unless NP=RP. We show that MSR admits deterministic polynomial-time exact recovery for every fixed $\gamma>1$, extending Gao and Reyzin's result for $\gamma\ge2$. All three results use the same Bilu--Linial stability model: the optimal partition remains uniquely optimal when each pairwise distance is multiplied by any factor in $[1,\gamma]$, without requiring the perturbed distances to satisfy the triangle inequality. The number of clusters is part of the input. For $1<\gamma<2$, our algorithm runs in $n^{O((\gamma-1)^{-5})}$ time.
The main structural insight is that a cheap merge in one part of the instance would allow a profitable split elsewhere under a suitable perturbation, contradicting stability. The resulting exchange inequality controls local cluster density, which gives linear growth and hence bounded treewidth in local interaction graphs. We use random partitions to obtain these regions, solve them by dynamic programming, and then derandomize the construction. For rational input and fixed rational $\gamma>1$, recognizing stability in this model is coNP-complete. Verifying that a supplied partition remains uniquely optimal under all allowed perturbations is coNP-complete for both arbitrary symmetric and metric perturbations.

title: FADE: Factored Ability--Difficulty Filtering for Online RLVR Scheduling
abstract: Group-based reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) learns only from prompts whose sampled completions disagree: all-pass and all-fail groups produce zero relative advantage and burn generation budget without moving the policy. Adaptive schedulers try to steer rollouts toward informative prompts, yet they rely on per-prompt pass-rate trackers that entangle two quantities evolving at very different speeds---the policy's shifting competence across reasoning skills and each prompt's intrinsic difficulty. When a single exponential average or Beta counter tracks both at once, short memory scrambles the relative ordering of prompts whereas long memory reports stale pass rates. We introduce FADE (Factored Ability--Difficulty Estimation), a bilinear state-space filter that separates the two timescales. FADE represents each prompt's success logit as the inner product of a whitened $K$-dimensional skill loading with a fast-drifting policy ability vector, minus a slow-shrinking scalar item intercept. Using Pólya--Gamma augmentation, each minibatch of binary rollout outcomes updates the $K$-dimensional ability posterior in closed form via a rank-$K$ Woodbury step, instantly transferring competence shifts to all unobserved prompts that share those skills while leaving item intercepts stable. From the resulting posterior mean and variance we derive a closed-form utility for the probability of drawing a non-degenerate rollout group. Across five reasoning benchmarks, two base models, and four scheduling paradigms under a matched rollout budget, FADE consistently improves downstream accuracy and calibration while adding less than $0.6$\,ms per step.

title: SpikePID: Real-Time Neuromorphic Cluster Counting in Future Drift Chambers
subjects: Instrumentation and Detectors (physics.ins-det); Hardware Architecture (cs.AR); High Energy Physics - Experiment (hep-ex)
abstract: Cluster counting ($dN/dx$) measures discrete ionization occurrences along a charged particle track traversing a gaseous medium and is currently being proposed to serve particle identification (PID) in next-generation drift chambers, as it is expected to offer higher separation power than the traditional approach based on the ionization energy loss measurement ($dE/dx$), which has intrinsically larger statistical fluctuations. However, measuring $dN/dx$ in drift chambers proposed for future colliders requires high-resolution waveforms, which result in very large data rates. Running the reconstruction at the edge would drastically reduce the bandwidth required to transmit data off the detector. In this paper, we introduce SpikePID, a neuromorphic computing approach applying spiking neural networks (SNNs) to this task due to their inherently sparse computing and processing nature. We show that an SNN with only 529 parameters improves the kaon-pion separation power by 17% over the traditional derivative-based method and by 4% over an MLP that has $8.6\times$ more parameters. When synthesized to an FPGA, it uses an order of magnitude fewer resources than the MLP, and has an inference latency compatible with the constraints of future collider experiments, making the SNN an excellent algorithmic candidate for real-time data readout in future drift chambers.

title: Inverse modelling of a laser-plasma accelerator
subjects: Accelerator Physics (physics.acc-ph); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Plasma Physics (physics.plasm-ph)
abstract: The electron beams of a laser-plasma accelerator depend non-linearly on the laser and gas settings. This dependence is explored using particle-in-cell (PIC) simulations, and machine-learning models trained on these simulations predict the beam from the settings. Here we address the reverse problem: given a measured beam, which settings produced it? We infer three of them: the gas pressure $p\_1$, the normalised vector potential $a\_0$ and the nitrogen concentration $c\_{N\_2}$. The solution is not guaranteed to be unique. We train an ensemble of mixture density networks that, for each beam, output several possible sets of settings with their probabilities and uncertainties, and test them on simulated beams with realistic measurement noise. On average, the predictions are accurate ($R^2 = 0.91$), yet for about two-thirds of the beams the inferred distribution has two competing solutions. These share nearly the same value of $a\_0^2 p\_1$, which controls how strongly the laser focuses itself in the plasma and, in earlier PALLAS studies, when electrons start to be injected. Keeping this quantity fixed gives beams that are practically indistinguishable with realistic diagnostics. A forward model used as a check removes unphysical solutions but cannot choose between the two plausible ones. We then test two ways to resolve the ambiguity. Adding the full electron energy spectrum improves the mean prediction ($R^2 = 0.94$), mostly through $a\_0$. It changes the weights of the two solutions but does not move them. A second measurement at a deliberately different plasma density is more effective. In paired PIC simulations, it reduces the error on $a\_0$ by a factor of 2.6, whereas repeating the measurement at the same density brings almost no gain.

title: A GPU-Accelerated and Geometry-Aware Quantum-Classical Framework for Optimized PES Scans with CUDA-Q
abstract: Hybrid quantum-classical workloads, particularly Potential Energy Surface (PES) scans in quantum chemistry using batched VQE and QAOA, involve many structurally similar Hamiltonians differing only in coefficients. Existing warm-start and meta-optimization strategies reuse parameters between instances but still consume fixed quantum-classical resources, ignoring cross-instance structural similarities. We present OptiPESS, a GPU-accelerated runtime system for adaptive resource allocation in hybrid quantum-classical execution. OptiPESS introduces the Locality-Occupancy-Variance (LOV) metric, a lightweight, geometry-aware measure of Hamiltonian similarity, coupled with efficient alignment and Pauli-classification passes. Using LOV, OptiPESS performs distance-aware scheduling of iteration and shot budgets, predicting which instances can be skipped, quick-solved, or fully optimized. Implemented atop CUDA-Q with persistent multi-GPU execution and near-linear scaling, OptiPESS reduces classical and quantum evaluations by up to 78.3\% and wall-time by up to 74.8\% while maintaining baseline accuracy. This demonstrates how lightweight static analysis and adaptive scheduling can transform quantum-classical co-execution from fixed-budget loops into a predictive, resource-aware runtime.

title: Reinforcement Learning in High-Energy Physics: A Survey from Accelerator Control to Theory Exploration
subjects: High Energy Physics - Experiment (hep-ex); Machine Learning (cs.LG); High Energy Physics - Phenomenology (hep-ph)
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a machine learning paradigm in which an agent learns a decision-making policy by interacting with an environment, guided by a scalar reward rather than explicit supervision. Supervised and unsupervised learning have become indispensable tools in high-energy physics (HEP), but they learn from fixed datasets, whereas many HEP tasks are closed-loop decisions: the data an algorithm observes depend on its choices, the feedback is sparse or delayed, and the objective is often measured on a real machine or in a stochastic simulation, not by a differentiable model. This survey reviews the application of RL to such tasks: accelerator control and feedback, data quality monitoring, jet grooming, clustering, and representation, charged particle tracking, beyond-the-Standard-Model (BSM) and string model building, detector design, trigger control, analysis, and formal quantum field theory computation. It provides a self-contained introduction to the underlying RL methods, from model-free and model-based to multi-agent, offline, inverse, and bandit approaches, reviews each domain against its traditional methods, and summarizes the head-to-head comparisons. The applications range from policies deployed on real accelerators and evaluated on recorded collision data to exploratory studies in formal theory. RL is most advantageous for repeated tasks with a fast simulator, decisions inside fast control loops, operation under faults and corrupted measurements, physics-based rewards in place of labels, and sequential discrete constructions with a reusable policy, while Bayesian optimization, genetic algorithms, and differentiable methods remain competitive elsewhere. We conclude with the open challenges that recur across domains, including reward design, sim-to-real transfer, safety, the lack of shared benchmarks, and the statistical validity of policy-driven decisions.
